A Nigerian man identified as Ayomide posed as a woman called Ava on TikTok to lure a Canadian teenager into sending nude pictures before threatening to publish them unless he paid, an investigation by the Associated Press has revealed. The investigation, conducted by the AP and PBS documentary programme FRONTLINE, was published on Tuesday. It exposed how the young Nigerian used fake identities and online messaging platforms to sexually blackmail teenage boys abroad. The Canadian teenager, who is now 18, told the AP that he was 15 when Ava first followed him on TikTok. Believing he was communicating with a woman, he exchanged messages with the account before being persuaded to move their conversation to Zangi, an encrypted messaging application. Ayomide, who is in his early 20s, reportedly sent the boy a nude photograph he had copied from the internet, claiming it was his own, before persuading him to send an intimate picture in return. He then threatened to share the teenager’s photograph with his family, friends and employer unless he paid. The victim initially sent $500, hoping to end the blackmail, but Ayomide continued demanding money. “Not just yet. This isn’t that simple,” Ayomide reportedly replied when the teenager asked if they could go their separate ways after the first payment. The AP said it met Ayomide in Lagos, where he shared chat histories of some of his scams, including conversations with the Canadian victim. The teenager was contacted after turning 18 and spoke on condition of anonymity because of the traumatic experience. The investigation reviewed more than 200 WhatsApp messages Ayomide sent to the victim, including threats to expose his identity and publish his intimate photograph. In one message, Ayomide threatened to disappoint the teenager’s mother by sharing the pictures online. He also sent him screenshots of his TikTok followers and personal identification details to reinforce the threats. The teenager eventually stopped responding to the messages after making what he described as a final payment. Ayomide continued sending threats, including more than 100 WhatsApp messages over 11 days, but the victim refused to engage. The AP reported that Ayomide said he never published the teenager’s photograph. He claimed to have received a few hundred dollars from him, while the victim estimated that he had paid close to $2,000. The news agency said it could not independently verify the total because neither party had comprehensive payment records. Ayomide, in a video posted by AP on YouTube, told the news agency that he felt bad about his actions and would apologise to the victim if given the opportunity. “Scamming is not good. I do feel bad. But as a man, you have to make money,” he said. He said he turned to internet fraud to meet his financial needs, including paying his rent and school fees. He described himself as a computer science student who was also apprenticing at a barbershop and said he hoped to become an engineer and work in the aviation industry. However, the investigation found that he had continued scamming. About a year after promising to stop, he had joined a group of other Yahoo Boys at his university. He declined to explain why he was still involved in the activity. The AP investigation described Ayomide as part of a growing network of online scammers, popularly known as Yahoo Boys in Nigeria, who target young people in Western countries through social media platforms. Financial sextortion involves criminals coercing victims into sharing nude images or videos before threatening to distribute the material unless they pay. According to the investigation, Ayomide followed hundreds of foreign men and boys on TikTok, posing as an attractive woman and engaging those who followed him back. He then moved conversations to private messaging platforms, where he could continue the manipulation and blackmail. He told the AP that for every 50 people he followed on TikTok, about 10 followed him back, while five were willing to chat. He also used Apple and Steam gift cards to collect payments, which he converted into local currency through a gift-card resale application. The investigation further found that he used PayPal accounts belonging to money mules recruited through WhatsApp. The AP said it provided PayPal with three accounts Ayomide had used to extort victims. The company said the accounts had been restricted shortly after they were created. The investigation also found that the Canadian teenager’s experience was part of a wider increase in financially motivated sextortion targeting minors, particularly boys. By August, the National Centre for Missing & Exploited Children had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion, compared with 50,000 reports throughout the previous year, according to the AP. The FBI has warned of the growing threat, while cybersecurity experts say the crime can have devastating consequences for victims. The investigation cited cases of teenagers who died by suicide after being blackmailed. An FBI law enforcement attaché in Abuja, Charles Smith, warned that the crime could affect any child with access to a computer or the internet. “These perpetrators are becoming more and more aggressive,” he said. “It can happen to any of our children, any child with access to a computer or online.” The AP also reported that the Nigerian Economic and Financial Crimes Commission had worked with US law enforcement on efforts to tackle transnational cybercrime. EFCC Chairman Olanipekun Olukoyede told the news agency that Nigeria would not remain a safe haven for fraudsters. “Rest assured, Nigeria is no longer going to be a safe haven for fraudsters or criminal activities,” he said. The investigation found that despite enforcement efforts, many scammers continued operating. The Canadian teenager told the AP that he remained haunted by the experience nearly two years after escaping Ayomide’s threats. However, when another scammer later approached him online using a fake female identity, he recognised the tactic, blocked the account and refused to engage. Ayomide, meanwhile, declined to comment on why he had continued scamming after previously saying he would quit.
